# Capacity Network Design {.unnumbered}

A greedy algorithm to explore interactions between the competing operational objectives in deciding how blood donation collection appointments (slots) should be distributed geographically.

# Overview

## Themes / Analytical methods

_R, prescriptive analytics, Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis, Computational statistics/Numerical methods, leaflet choropleth geo-mapping, conveying abstract concepts to decision-makers_

## Business Problem

### Problem statement
The organisation's current operational setup for blood donation collection is not optimised. Appointments (slots) are not optimally distributed in either a spatial or temporal sense i.e. people who are willing and able to donate blood cannot always find a slot near them, at a suitable time. What would the collection capacity network looked like if we rebuilt it from scratch in the optimal way?

### Academic Aim
A numerical method by way of a greedy algorithm that, given a set of organisational objectives along with relative weights or priorities, allocates a given number of appointments geographically so as to maximise the likelihood of meeting those objectives.

## Scoping and planning

* I decided to consider an optimisation problem with respect to only the spatial distributiion of slots, as a first step. I recognised that the temporal aspect could be dealt with independently, because I had no reason to believe that the optimal temporal distribution should be significantly different between geographical areas - as such the problem could be reduced to two independent optimisation problems, of which I would tackle the spatial one in the first instance.
* I recognised this as an application for Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis (MCDA), especially considering the difficulty of expressing different organisational objectives in comparable terms e.g. collecting enough blood from Black African and Black Caribbean donors, and minimising the distance collected blood needs to travel to manufacturing sites

## Limitations
* Numerical methods are liable to fail to converge or converge on a local optimum rather than a global optimum, but given their ability to approach otherwise untractable problems and compute in a reasonable time, the use is justified here, as detailed below.

## Technical choices

* I recognised that the optimal solution would be a function of the ordering or weighting of the competing orgnisational objectives, and so chose to use a computational approach of an algorithm that incrementally added capacity to the next-best location at each step (greedy) by using an objective function that was a weighted average of "monetised" or otherwise quantified organisational objectives
* I decided that a solution that conveyed the above mechanic, that the weighting/priority strongly determined the optimum, was more important to convey to decision-makers than converging on a contrived or otherwise arbitrary "objective" optimum. As such, I felt justified in using an approach that can sometimes miss the global optimum.
* The computational approach with the weighted objective function also allowed me to
  * demonstrate with fine control how tweaking or varying the weighted shifted the optimum in the direction of different extremes, to non-technical decision makers
  * compute and compare different scenarios side by side
* As a proof of concept (POC) I developed a Shiny app with inputs for parameters to demonstrate the reduction of the problem down to the weighted objectives

## Validation

As the algorithm is a simulation, there is no operational or historical data to compare it with. Instead, as demonstrated in @example, a key step of the evaluation of results is to sense-check and rationalise the observations as parameters are varied and scenarios are compared. Because of the fine-tune control over the algorithm and its deterministic nature, it is possible to determine the effect of each parameter or iteration loop in the algorithm as necessary: It can be re-run and paused after each loop, or it can be run with a tweaked parameter.

## Impact  

This work enabled senior decision-makers to fully grasp the reduction of the problem into a weighting/ordering of organisational objectives. This was facilitated by the proof of concept Shiny app and the leaflet choropleths. They allowed me to convey that there was no objective correct answer to the problem, but instead the priorities that were input, via the objective function, would allow the algorithm to prescribe a capacity allocation that would best fulfil them.

# Project code & Output

In lieu of a link to the repo, which is not public, the below explores the architecture, pseudocode, excerpts, and outputs relating to the repo and project.

The codebase of the project consists of:
* a POC Shiny app to demonstrate the greedy algorithm in this context
* an R script with a more sophisticated objective function, which outputs a choropleth leaflet map for the optimal slot distribution at a constituency granularity.

# Relevance to the Senior Data Scientist role

The problem of weighing up inherently uncomparable or non-monetary objectives is one that all public sector organisations face. As such, the role of computational methods and MCDA in prescriptive analytics is highly transferrable. This could include distributing resources, care, workforce geographically, or allocating funding between them.  

# What I learnt / would improve

A key source of non-progress surrounded the hesistance of stakeholders to commit to a weighting/ordering of priority of objectives. Next time, I would conduct a sensitivity analysis to understand the effect on the output (allocation) that a unit change in weightings would cause. This would at least prescribe a sensible precision for the weightings, which it occured to me might make the task less daunting for decision-makers e.g. if they knew the weightings only needed to be in 10% blocks rather than 1% blocks.
